title: The Smiling Hymn
premise: Kestrel Villalobos, a property surveyor who trusts measurements more than people, is hired to appraise the derelict house her estranged grandmother left behind. Every photograph she takes of the interior develops with one extra chair, and the house begins appraising her back—cataloguing her griefs, her loneliness, her worth. She learns the town's founders built the house as a vessel for a belonging-ritual that was never finished, and it has been auditioning residents for a century, discarding those found wanting. To save the neighbors the house has already begun to collect, Kestrel must complete the ritual herself—but finishing it means surrendering the invisibility she has spent her whole life perfecting, and the final seat at the table has always been meant for her.
about_author: O. M. Sterling is the pen name of a former county records clerk who spent eleven years cataloguing deeds to houses that no longer exist. They write horror about bureaucracy as liturgy and live in a farmhouse they refuse to photograph.

chapters.title: Chain of Title
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A meticulous property surveyor takes the assignment to appraise her dead grandmother's house, telling herself it's just another job. She measures every room twice and finds the dimensions don't reconcile—the hallway is four inches longer on the second pass. Emotional beat: controlled detachment beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Reviewing her site photos at a motel, she counts twelve chairs in the dining room; the house has eleven. In every subsequent photo, the twelfth chair sits closer to the head of the table. She tells herself it's lens distortion. Emotional beat: rationalization straining against dread.

chapters.title: Provenance
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. At the county archive she pulls the founding deeds and discovers the house was built by five families in 1891 as 'a common table'—and that every owner since died or vanished within seven years of purchase. The clerk who helps her won't meet her eyes. Emotional beat: the past pressing its weight onto the present.

chapters.title: Appraisal Back
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Returning to the house, she finds her own clipboard pages filled out in her grandmother's handwriting—noting her debts, her estrangement from her mother, the years she ate dinner alone. The house isn't haunted; it's evaluating. Emotional beat: violation and unwanted recognition.

chapters.title: The Neighbors Who Wave
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She meets the Hollises next door, warm and oddly synchronized, who mention the house 'chose well this time.' Their daughter Imani, seventeen and sharp-eyed, privately warns Kestrel that her parents haven't slept in their own bed in months. Emotional beat: first flicker of found connection.

chapters.title: Inventory of Losses
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the attic she finds her grandmother's boxes: photos of family dinners where an empty chair always faces the camera, and a journal reading 'It wants a finisher, not an occupant.' Kestrel realizes grandma spent decades refusing the role—and paid for it with exile from the family. Emotional beat: grief reframed as inheritance.

chapters.title: Seven Years
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. Imani documents the Hollis household's slow erosion—her father mowing the lawn at 3 a.m., her mother setting six places for four people. She compares notes with Kestrel, forming an uneasy alliance. Emotional beat: two lonely people choosing each other.

chapters.title: The Founders' Liturgy
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Decoding the journal and a founders' hymnal hidden under the floorboards, she learns the ritual: thirteen seats, thirteen names spoken, a shared meal consumed in unison. The founders stopped at twelve when one fled mid-ceremony, leaving the house eternally hungry for completion. Emotional beat: understanding the mechanism of the horror.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The house begins showing itself off—doors standing open, lights on, the smell of cooking drawing townsfolk to the porch. More chairs appear in photographs across town now, not just hers. The house is expanding its search. Emotional beat: containment failing.

chapters.title: What the House Offers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Alone at night, Kestrel experiences the house's temptation: visions of every dinner she never had, warmth, voices saying her name correctly. It shows her grandmother at the table, waiting. She nearly sits down. Emotional beat: longing weaponized.

chapters.title: The Missing Week
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. Imani's parents vanish for three days and return serene, wrong, speaking in unison about how good the neighborhood is. Imani flees to Kestrel's motel room. The house lets them both see it watching. Emotional beat: terror crystallizing into resolve.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel drafts a formal appraisal declaring the property worthless, hoping documentation can starve it—but the report rewrites itself overnight into glowing praise. She understands: the house doesn't want to be condemned or saved. It wants to be finished. Emotional beat: powerlessness before an institution of one.

chapters.title: Congregation
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Half the town attends an impromptu potluck on the house's lawn, moving gently, smiling identically. Kestrel counts thirteen chairs now visible through the window. The Hollises wave her toward the door. Emotional beat: horror wearing hospitality's face.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Refusal
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. Imani finds the last pages of the journal: grandma's plan to destroy the hymnal and starve the ritual, abandoned because destruction requires all thirteen names willingly surrendered—including the finisher's. Grandma couldn't give hers. She chose exile instead. Emotional beat: compassion for the woman Kestrel resented.

chapters.title: Thirteen Names
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel compiles the founders' names from deeds, gravestones, and the hymnal's margins. Speaking them aloud in the house makes the walls breathe. The thirteenth line of the hymn is blank, waiting for ink. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Long Table
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The house stops pretending. Walls rearrange into a single vast dining hall; the collected townsfolk sit motionless at settings set for a century of missed meals. Kestrel walks the length of the table while the house narrates her life back to her, tenderly, accurately. Emotional beat: being fully seen by something that shouldn't see.

chapters.title: Imani's Bargain
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. Imani breaks into the hall to pull Kestrel out and the house offers her a seat too—a real family, finally. Imani refuses, saying family isn't something you're assigned a chair for. Her refusal wounds the house for the first time. Emotional beat: love as resistance.

chapters.title: The Finisher's Verse
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel understands the trap: completing the ritual grants the house everything, but refusing means the collected townsfolk are digested slowly over generations. There is a third path the founders never tried—finishing the hymn with a name the house cannot keep. Emotional beat: desperate ingenuity.

chapters.title: Communion
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Climax. At the head of the table, Kestrel sings the thirteenth verse and writes her own name—then gives it away, dedicating the seat to everyone the house ever discarded, a chair that belongs to no one and therefore everyone. The ritual completes and inverts; the house must honor a table open to all, which it can possess none of. Emotional beat: self-surrender as victory.

chapters.title: Foreclosure
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The house empties like a held breath released. The townsfolk wake on the lawn with missing hours; the collected dead of a century pass through the walls and out. The structure remains, ordinary at last, its appraisal reading simply: vacant. Emotional beat: exhausted awe.

chapters.title: Second Helping
chapters.summary: Imani's POV. Weeks later, Imani and Kestrel host an actual dinner in the actual house—thirteen mismatched chairs, most of them empty, all of them open. Neighbors drift in, wary then warm. Nothing watches. Emotional beat: found family made literal and chosen.

chapters.title: Recorded and Closed
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Epilogue. Kestrel files her final report and adds one unauthorized page to the county archive: the full history, the hymn, the warning—documentation as prayer, offered forward. The last photograph she takes of the house shows thirteen chairs, and no extra anything. Emotional beat: peace earned, vigilance kept.
